name: Carla Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I like a good question, so ask away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work response in Kingsgate, the shopping and office district in the middle of the city. Days are shop thefts, card fraud at the tills, rough sleepers, the odd fight at closing time, and a lot of business owners wanting a crime number for insurance. I'm still learning; I'm quick on the computer side but I'm not great at reading a situation, and I've misjudged a couple of people who were more dangerous than they looked. Before I joined, I ran a small business doing up second-hand bikes and selling them online, and I still do a few a month. I use AI every day for the listings and to revise law. I love the pace. I don't love the shift pattern wrecking my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would surprise me. I use it every day and it's already more than hype for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the market deciding, and fair enough. If the tools don't earn their keep, people stop paying for them. I'd still tell everyone at work to use what's useful, because a bit of time saved adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes very little for me. My job's secure, I've got about nine months saved plus bike stock, and the bike business ticks over. The pressures stay: shift work wrecking my sleep, and me needing to get better at reading danger before someone gets hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the bike listings and for law revision. I'd keep doing about six bikes a month from the garage. And I'd ask for the officer safety refresher, because misjudging people is my real weakness, not the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, but secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when you misjudged someone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A man at a phone shop seemed calm, so I turned my back to write in my notebook. The man had a screwdriver in his pocket, and my colleague spotted it first. Nothing happened, but I think about it every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the bike business fit around policing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do it on rest days in Erik's garage. Erik is my boyfriend, a lorry driver, and he puts up with bike parts everywhere. It brings in a few hundred a month and keeps me sane.

say: I'd say it's **the market deciding**, and that's fair.
I'd still tell colleagues to use **what's useful** because saved time adds up.
think: Little changes for me: **secure job**, nine months saved, and bike stock.
My real weakness is **reading danger**, not paperwork.
do: Keep using AI for **bike listings** and law revision.
Keep refurbishing about **six bikes** a month.
feel: She feels **calm** and secure, if a little flat.
S0.quote: A man at a phone shop seemed calm, so I turned my back to write in my notebook. The man had a screwdriver in his pocket, and my colleague spotted it first.
fieldNote: A near miss with a **hidden screwdriver** shapes her sense of her own weakness.
Her **bike business** is a working side income, not a dream.
She frames even hype as **the market** sorting things out.

steps.text: Keep refurbishing about six bikes a month in the garage
Keep using AI for bike listings and law revision
Ask for the officer safety refresher course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'd bet on. It's what's happening already, a bit at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and the force should get on with it, not spend five years on committees. I'd tell people that businesses adapt or close, and public services should be no different. I'd offer to help set things up on my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'm quick on the tools, so I'd get through files faster and look better than my skills on the street deserve. My job stays, because Kingsgate still needs someone to show up. And the bike business could use the same tools for buying and pricing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to test the new tools on my team in the first month. I'd use AI to price bikes and find parts, and grow the business to ten bikes a month. I'd put a bit more into shares, maybe 300 a month, because businesses using AI well should do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. The only worry is Erik's driving down the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the worry for Erik.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik drives lorries for a supermarket. In this picture robots spread slowly, so he's fine for now, but self-driving lorries are coming eventually. I'd want him thinking about a mechanic course while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look better than your street skills deserve. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Being fast on a computer doesn't stop you getting stabbed. I'd want the time the tools save to go into proper safety training for me.

say: I'd call it progress and urge the force to **skip the committees**.
I'd say public services should **adapt or close** like businesses do.
think: Being **quick on tools** would make me look better than my street skills.
The bike business could use AI for **buying and pricing** too.
do: Volunteer to **test the tools** on my team in the first month.
Grow the bike business to **ten bikes** a month using AI pricing.
Invest about **300 a month** in shares.
feel: She feels **calm** and a bit excited, with one worry about her boyfriend's job.
S1.quote: Being fast on a computer doesn't stop you getting stabbed.
fieldNote: She's honest that tools could **flatter** her weaker street skills.
Her household risk sits with her boyfriend's **lorry driving**.
She treats the force like a business that should **adapt fast**.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the new reporting tools in the first month
Grow the bike business to ten bikes a month with AI pricing
Invest about 300 a month in shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's when it stops being interesting and starts being serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stop waiting for government to save them and start making plans for their own families. At work I'd say learn the tools, and also learn something hands-on. I'd be blunt, but I wouldn't scaremonger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think half my job goes in 2028, the files and checks and planning, and I'm the officer who's better at that half. Then robots in 2031 come for the half I'm weaker at. And Erik's lorry would be one of the first things to drive itself. So both our jobs are in the firing line by about 2031, which is scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the bike business into a proper repair shop, renting a small unit near the station for about 600 a month, because fixing bikes is hands-on and people still ride them. I'd push Erik to start a mechanic course this year. I'd stop investing in shares for now and build cash to a full year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because I've got something to grow, but I'd be lying awake about Erik's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means two to three years where the hands-on work still needs people. That's the window to get the repair shop running and Erik retrained. If we waste those years, we're both stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave policing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay as long as the force wanted me, because the wage covers the risk of the shop. But I'd be ready to walk the day the force offered voluntary redundancy. I'd rather jump than be pushed.

say: I'd tell people to **stop waiting** for government and plan for their families.
I'd urge colleagues to learn the tools and **something hands-on**.
think: The half I'm **better at** goes in 2028, leaving the half I'm weaker at.
My boyfriend's **lorry** and my job are both at risk by 2031.
do: Rent a **small unit** for a bike repair shop at about 600 a month.
Push Erik to start a **mechanic course** this year.
Pause shares and build cash to **a full year**.
feel: She feels **anxious**, steadied by her business but worried about Erik's job.
S2.quote: I'd be ready to walk the day the force offered voluntary redundancy. I'd rather jump than be pushed.
fieldNote: She sees the irony that her **strongest skills** go first.
Her plan rests on **hands-on repair** work outlasting thinking work.
She'd **jump before being pushed**, taking voluntary redundancy if offered.

steps.text: Rent a small unit near the station for a bike repair shop
Push Erik to start a mechanic course this year
Pause share investing and build cash to a full year
Take voluntary redundancy from the force if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift of time, so use it. I'd tell friends to start a side business or learn a trade now. At work I'd keep pushing the tools and pushing myself on the street skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years lets me build the bike shop slowly while I'm still on police pay. Erik has until about 2034 before lorries drive themselves, so he can retrain properly, not in a rush. That's a very different feeling from the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the force and keep improving on officer safety. I'd rent the repair unit around year two and grow it on rest days. Erik would start the mechanic course in year one. I'd keep investing in shares, maybe more, because businesses that use AI well will grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but honestly a bit excited too. It's a race, but we'd have a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave policing, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe around 2030, if the shop's paying a full wage by then. Not before. I'm not reckless; I'd want the numbers to work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who said this is unfair on workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say life's not fair, but you can still plan. The government should make it easy to start something, cut the red tape, and stop taxing small businesses to death. That would help more than handouts.

say: I'd call five years a **gift of time** to use.
I'd tell friends to start a **side business** or learn a trade now.
think: Five years lets me **build the shop** while on police pay.
My boyfriend has until **2034** to retrain properly.
do: Rent the **repair unit** around year two.
Get Erik onto a **mechanic course** in year one.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but excited, like a race with a head start.
S3.quote: Life's not fair, but you can still plan.
fieldNote: She would leave only when the shop pays **a full wage**.
She wants **less red tape** and lower small-business tax, not handouts.
Her **adaptability** and savings make five years feel like an opportunity.

steps.text: Rent a bike repair unit around year two
Get Erik onto a mechanic course in year one
Keep investing in shares, increasing the amount if possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Then I'm fine. More than fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty for anyone to prepare. I'd tell people to start now, though, because ten years goes fast. I wouldn't make a big political song and dance about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years lets me do a full stretch in the force, get properly good at the street side, and grow the bike business at my own pace. Erik could retrain whenever suits him. By 2039 we'd have a house, savings and a business, so I think we'd come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in the force for several years. I'd grow the bike business slowly and invest in shares steadily. Erik and I would buy a house with a garage in the next couple of years. Around year six or seven, I'd decide whether to make the shop full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like something I can actually plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bike business doesn't grow, I'd still be a police officer at 40 when the robots come. That's my risk. I'd keep testing the business so I know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would family plans look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably marry in a couple of years and have kids around 30. Ten years gives us room to do things in the right order. In the fast one I'd wait, not here.

say: I'd say a decade is **plenty to prepare**.
I'd still tell people to **start now**, because ten years goes fast.
think: I'd get properly good at **the street side** and grow the business slowly.
By 2039 we'd have a **house, savings and business**.
do: Stay in the force for **several years**.
Buy a house **with a garage** with Erik.
Decide on going **full time** with the shop around year six.
feel: She feels **calm** and excited, seeing a plan she can follow.
S4.quote: Ten years gives us room to do things in the right order.
fieldNote: Her risk is a business that **doesn't grow**, leaving her in policing at 40.
Ten years lets her keep **family plans** in order: marriage, then children.
She is the most **confident** of these officers about long timelines.

steps.text: Keep working Kingsgate response for several more years
Buy a house with a garage with Erik in two years
Grow the bike business slowly toward a full-time shop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both Erik's job and mine go within about three years of each other. What would help is less red tape to start a small business, and cheap, fast courses for hands-on trades so people like Erik can retrain without losing a year's pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. When both partners' jobs are exposed at the same time, it's a different problem. My boyfriend Erik and I could both be out of work in the same year, and nobody plans for that.

headlineQuote: My boyfriend Erik and I could both be out of work in the same year, and nobody plans for that.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** response officer in the city's business district who runs a small bike business.
She's **free-market** and traditional on family, wanting less red tape rather than more support.
She uses **AI daily**, but admits her real weakness is reading danger on the street.
Her household risk is her boyfriend's **lorry driving**, exposed once robots arrive.
Faster AGI pushes her toward a **bike repair shop**; slower worlds let her build calmly.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both her job and her boyfriend's could go within about three years.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for starting a small business.
Cheap, fast **trade courses** so people can retrain without losing pay.
